analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal financing for manufactured home parks on basic tenant rights like lease renewals, rent-increase notice, and the right to sell a home in place.
analysis.headline: Three Senate Democrats introduced the bill in March 2025; it was referred to the Banking Committee, where no hearing, vote, or further action has been taken since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would say no to federal backing for loans that build, substantially rehab, or buy manufactured home communities unless the owner promises, in writing and across all communities they own, a set of tenant protections. Residents would get one-year leases that renew unless there is good cause to refuse, at least 60 days' written notice (with justification) before any rent increase or new charge, a five-day grace period on rent, the right to sell their home where it stands rather than move it, and 60 days' notice before a sale or closure of the whole community, with a window in which tenants could try to buy it. Owners who break the rules could face paying tenants back with interest plus a penalty, or losing access to federal financing for at least two years.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live in manufactured home communities — households that typically own their home but rent the land under it — in communities financed through the covered federal programs. They would gain predictable leases, advance written notice and justification before rent increases or new charges, a short grace period on rent, the right to sell their home in place (including for a period after eviction), for-sale-sign rights, and first notice plus a negotiation window if the owner plans to sell or close the community. The protections would also reach every community owned by the same owner or affiliate, not just the financed property.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who rent their lots

how_it_helps.text: Any owner seeking a federally insured HUD loan or a loan bought by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac for a manufactured home community would first have to certify that every community they own (including affiliates' communities) gives tenants one-year renewable leases with good-cause limits on nonrenewal.

Rent increases and new charges require 60 days' written notice with a written justification showing operating-cost information; increases over 5 percent require an extra 30 days' notice for each additional 2.5 percent increase.

Residents get a 5-day grace period on rent, a 15-day right to cure a missed payment, the right to sell their home in place without moving it out of the community (including for 45 days after an eviction), the right to post a for-sale sign, and the right to assign the pad-site lease to a buyer unless the buyer fails reasonable, uniformly applied criteria.

Owners must give 60 days' advance notice before selling or closing the community, with the price and terms disclosed, and must negotiate in good faith if the tenants want to buy the community during that window.

The bill backs these rights with penalties, including repayments to tenants plus 25 percent for improper rent increases or late fees, months of rent for lease violations, and a two-year ban on future federal housing financing for willful violators.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of manufactured home communities — including large investors and portfolio owners — who rely on HUD-insured loans or loans sold to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac. They would have to rewrite standard leases to include the protections, document compliance, accept limits on raising rents, and pay defined penalties to tenants for violations, or forgo this federal financing entirely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Manufactured home park owners and investors

drawbacks.text: The protections apply only to communities whose owners borrow through these three federal loan programs; residents of communities financed privately, or whose owners simply avoid federal financing, get none of these rights.

Tying loans to tenant protections could make financing harder or costlier to obtain for buying, building, or rehabilitating communities, which owners could pass on through higher lot rents or which could reduce sales of communities to resident groups if conventional buyers decline the conditions.

Enforcement rests on borrowers certifying compliance and federal agencies policing documentation, so an owner facing a violation could restructure or shift financing rather than change practices, leaving the lease protections uneven across the sector.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: the bill would give residents of federally financed communities a stable one-year lease, advance notice before big rent increases, the ability to sell their home in place, and a shot at buying the community when it goes up for sale, backed by penalties with teeth. The main drawbacks are that the protections reach only communities whose owners use these three federal loan programs, so residents elsewhere are left out; and the conditions could make financing scarcer or more expensive for community purchases, which over time could pressure rents or push owners to sell to non-eligible buyers. The bill is well targeted at how the sector is actually financed, but its conditionality is an honest limit a supporter must acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late March 2025 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote ever since.

narrative.text: The only actions taken were introduction and referral to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on March 27, 2025; the full action history shows nothing after that.
The bill has three Senate cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further floor or committee activity.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, manufactured home community owners are better off: because the bill has not advanced, they can still obtain federally backed financing for building, buying, or rehabilitating communities without having to accept the bill's lease protections or penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of manufactured home communities, so far

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 27, 2025 and referred it to the Banking Committee.

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and John Fetterman
for.role: U.S. Senators from Connecticut and Pennsylvania

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral on March 27, 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no vote appears in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: All three original supporters are Democrats (3 of 45 Senate Democrats), no Republican cosponsors have signed on, and the Republican-led Banking Committee has taken no action since referral.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors (including REITs and private-equity-backed operators)
industries.note: Owners who rely on HUD-insured loans or Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac purchases would have to accept lease rules, notice requirements, tenant sale rights, and penalty payments that limit how fast they can raise rents or close communities. Because many park residents cannot afford to move their homes, owners currently hold strong bargaining power that this bill would trim.

industries.industry: Community mortgage lenders and loan brokers
industries.note: Lenders originate the federally backed loans that would become conditional, so some deals might shrink or slow if owners refuse the conditions, while others would simply add a compliance step.

industries.industry: HUD-insured manufactured home park lending and the Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac manufactured home community loan programs
industries.note: The bill adds a certification and documentation requirement to these programs and lets regulators cut off willful violators, so the programs would carry the rules that investors either accept or walk away from.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee activity and no Republican cosponsors, the usual path for a bill in this position is to remain in committee without a hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress unless its sponsor secures broader support or attaches the provisions to a larger housing bill.
